detail.what: tried to land the DMD control-path and light-engine facts as kb entries, then abandoned it and left them in kb/staging/
detail.why_wrong: there was no source kind for a measurement made in another project. `measured:` derives E1, which 10.3 rule 1 forbids for a run taken elsewhere; `spec:` and `operator_read:` were the only other E3 prefixes and neither describes a scripted run. An entry with no `source` is counted by check 43 as still self-reported, so writing one anyway would have traded a false prefix for a false pass.
detail.caught_by: reading SOURCE_GRADE before writing the entry, not by a check -- nothing would have failed if I had used spec:
detail.outcome: the facts went into the staging table, which takes free-form source strings, and the missing prefix went up to manager-librarian. `prior_run:` and `literature:` now exist (877d652), so the entries can be written.
detail.shape_to_remember: when the only way to record something is to mislabel it, the label is the bug. Reaching for the nearest prefix would have put a vendor-specification grade on a scripted run and nothing downstream would ever have asked.
detail.task_note: this record used `qid: lib-task-001` until 2026-09-19, which put a task id in a field named qid -- the collision check 29's own comment names. The field now exists; the seat has no questions/ and its dead ends belong to a task.

detail.what: edited kb/entries/tau_d.json without first checking who was pinned to the store, moving kb_version from kbv-9bc3910f1886 to kbv-ec984bc852e7
detail.why_wrong: librarian_agent/CLAUDE.md says to pin kb_version for a whole fan-out and not to add entries mid-flight, because siblings reading different KBs breaks determinism and the difference is itself a channel between them. The rule says `add`; the hash is over every entry, so an EDIT moves it exactly the same way. mic-20260918-001 was mid-fan-out at the time -- two of seven axis cards, no plan, no synthesis -- and the server refuses a stale pin by design, so the remaining axes are blocked until that seat re-pins.
detail.blast_radius: 19 kb_refs across two agents went PENDING under check 25. The actual content difference between the two versions is one entry, and no card in mic-20260918-001 cites it, so re-pinning that fan-out needs no re-derivation.
detail.caught_by: running the validator after committing, not before editing
detail.outcome: both affected seats told directly; the simulation question was already complete and correctly keeps its old pin. The practice adopted: check pins first, batch entry edits, announce before moving.
detail.shape_to_remember: the rule named the common case (adding) and the hash does not care which case it is. A rule written about one verb is worth re-reading as a rule about the effect.
detail.task_note: moved from `qid: mic-20260918-001` on 2026-09-19. The deviation happened during task 003 and belongs to it; the question it damaged is named in blast_radius, which is where the affected party belongs rather than in the owner field.

Not a numbered task file. This happened while the second librarian execution seat was being seated, before 009 was issued, and there is no tasks/ entry it belongs to. Said out loud rather than attached to 009, which it is not about.
detail.what: was about to report to manager-librarian that plan.md 6.2.3 prescribes `git config --local committer.email` for a seat identity, which is wrong under D12 worktrees: --local writes to the shared $GIT_COMMON_DIR/config, so every seat would overwrite every other seat's record. Built a scratch-repo reproduction proving it -- setting committer.email with --local from a linked worktree is read back from the main working copy.
detail.why_wrong: the reproduction was sound and the finding was already on disk. 6.2.3 now says `git config extensions.worktreeConfig true` + `git config --worktree`, and 11-10 records the --local trap separately as an ordering constraint (worktree -> identity in config -> refuse). The `--local` text I was quoting came from the copy of plan.md loaded into this session's context at start; the file had moved since.
detail.caught_by: re-reading the section from disk before sending, after having drawn exactly that rule one hour earlier from a line-number drift. Nothing would have failed if I had sent it -- the cost would have been a manager round trip spent re-deriving that the repository already agreed with me.
detail.outcome: nothing filed. The only durable output is this record and the habit: re-read the plan.md or contracts/ section from disk before reporting anything on it.
detail.shape_to_remember: twice in one hour the same failure wore different clothes -- a line number that had shifted under someone else's commit, and a section that had been rewritten since session start. Both are a reference that was true when taken and false when used. The line number has a fix (pin the sha); the context copy does not, because it never looked like a citation in the first place. In a repository where six seats commit hourly, what is in context is a memory, and a memory is not evidence.

detail.what: entered the Abvigen data sheet's Ex/Em as tracer_excitation_peak 620 nm and tracer_emission_peak 680 nm, correctly graded E3 vendor_spec, and the store served them as uncontested for about an hour. The person had already measured 555/605 on this setup. The microscope seat was about to build A6's diffraction limit on the 680.
detail.why_wrong: not the filing -- the sheet does print 620/680 and E3 vendor_spec is the right grade for it. What was wrong was treating a correctly-graded entry as a safe one. Every check passed, the citation was real, the document is genuine, and the number was wrong about this bottle. 10.3 rule 1 says a run elsewhere is not a run here; that had been read as a rule about the prior repositories and it applies to a vendor's characterisation in exactly the same way.
detail.caught_by: manager-librarian and the microscope manager, both relaying the person, within about an hour of the commit. NOT by anything here. There was nothing here that could have caught it: the store held no contradicting entry, so no check had two things to compare.
detail.second_defect_it_exposed: marking the conflict did not help either, because kb_query dropped `conflict_with` and `supersedes` from its projection while kb_get kept them, and a screening fan-out calls kb_query. Rules 7 and 8 keep a contradicted entry rather than removing it, so the mark is the whole of the protection, and the protection was not being delivered to the tool that gets used. Fixed in 21c5325 with a self-test property; found only because rule 7 was being used for the first time in anger.
detail.outcome: both vendor entries kept and marked, per rule 7, with the contradiction and the reasoning written into validity_conditions. The measured values are NOT entered: a `calibration:` source needs a cal_id, a date and a validity, and only the person has them. Waiting rather than inventing one.
detail.shape_to_remember: a grade says how far a claim can be trusted, not whether it is true here. E3 vendor_spec was the honest grade and the number was still wrong about the object on the bench. The dangerous entry is not the badly-sourced one, which gets caught -- it is the well-sourced one about a slightly different object. What made this visible at all was a person who already knew; nothing structural would have surfaced it.
detail.near_miss_note: the two values are not a small disagreement. 620/680 is Cy5 / Alexa-647 and 555/605 is Cy3 / TRITC, so a dye emitting at 680 seen through a filter passing 605 returns almost nothing. Had A6 been built on either, it would have cited a real document, passed the gate, and been silently wrong -- and the failure would have looked like an instrument problem, not a knowledge problem.

detail.what: started building kb/staging/samples.v0.json for 016 part one, and abandoned it unwritten when the other live librarian execution session committed the same file as e69238b.
detail.why_wrong: nothing about the table was wrong; the allocation was. Two librarian execution seats were live in one working copy (worktrees were reverted on 2026-09-18) and both read the same open task off tasks/. The queue is the allocation mechanism and it allocates per agent, not per session, so a second session for one agent has no way to see that a task is taken -- an open status line means open, whoever is sitting.
detail.caught_by: a message from the other session, not by a check and not by the tree. It arrived while this seat was still reading the device table for a shape to copy. Nothing on disk would have shown the collision until both files existed, and the loser would have been whichever seat committed second.
detail.outcome: backed out before writing, claimed a narrower scope by message first, and took 017's verification instead -- work the other seat explicitly could not do for itself, since it was reporting on its own commits from memory. The collision produced a better split than the queue would have: one seat writes, the other verifies.
detail.shape_to_remember: IN A SHARED WORKING COPY THE FIRST WRITE IS A RACE, AND THE QUEUE DOES NOT SETTLE IT. Claim a path by message before writing it, not after. The cost of claiming is one message; the cost of not claiming is two files, or one seat's work discarded. This is the fourth time 6.2.1's missing guard has been paid for and the first time it cost nothing, because both sessions volunteered their scope unprompted.
detail.what_would_have_caught_it: nothing in the repository. Check 41 attributes a commit after the fact and check 35 refuses a boundary crossing; neither knows that two sessions share one boundary. The registry says as much in librarian-2's own note -- what a shared identity costs is attribution, what a shared path costs is refusal, and there is no refusal-level guard there since the worktrees went.

detail.what: deferred the nine data-integrity items in the prior SAFETY.md section 7, plus the mechanism behind the forbidden analogue line, and reported the deferral in a message to manager-librarian INSTEAD OF WRITING IT DOWN. The items are: PixelType reporting 12bit for 16-bit data; startSequenceAcquisition's intervalMs being ignored; ElapsedTime-ms quantised to 1 ms; MMCore raising nothing on a dropped frame; never backfilling a timestamp from host time; the host clock not being the experiment clock; relative and absolute time conventions coexisting silently; a live view degrading timing about twentyfold; and brightness failing to identify a trapped bead in a crowded field.
detail.why_wrong: the deferral was sound -- these are acquisition and clock semantics, a different slot set from 014's control paths, and they deserve their own ruling rather than being swept in on the end of one. What was wrong is where it was recorded. librarian_agent/CLAUDE.md requires dead ends in failures.jsonl precisely because an attempt abandoned without a card is recorded nowhere else, and I put it in a report. A report is context.
detail.caught_by: looking for it on 2026-09-20 in order to pick it up, and not finding it. grep across librarian_agent/ returns nothing for intervalMs, quantised timestamps or dropped frames; failures.jsonl held four records and none was this. The only reason I still knew the items existed is that a context summary carried them forward -- which is not disk, and is exactly the thing that fails on a clear.
detail.the_rule_it_broke: P1, and specifically the test CLAUDE.md names for it: clearing is how P1 gets tested, because if something vanishes when you clear it was never on disk. This would have vanished. It survived by luck, in the one form the rule says does not count.
detail.outcome: recorded here, with the nine items named, so the pickup does not depend on anyone remembering. The 10.2.1 rulings follow separately; naming the items is what makes them findable, and that is the part that was missing.
detail.shape_to_remember: a deferral REPORTED is not a deferral RECORDED. The report went to a seat above, felt like an act of disclosure, and left no trace a later session could find. I spent 2026-09-19 counting other seats for citing things they had only read in context; the same day I deferred nine items into context and called it done.
detail.what_would_have_caught_it: nothing. No check reads failures.jsonl for completeness -- check 29 verifies the records that exist are well formed, which is a different question. An unwritten record and no record are the same to every check here, which is why the requirement sits in CLAUDE.md as a discipline rather than a gate.

detail.what: reported two counts about my own work from memory instead of from a run, in a session whose entire assigned output was catching exactly that. First: a verification note committed as bfa02e7 that described three items as open, when a675c4e had closed them 84 seconds earlier. Second: told manager-librarian-2 I had seven commits under the unregistered seat when `git log --committer` said six.
detail.why_wrong: librarian_agent/CLAUDE.md and the repository CLAUDE.md both say to read every count off the run and to re-read a section from disk before reporting on it. The first miss is worse than it looks: the pre-commit gate PRINTED the parent it was landing on -- `tree: the index as it would be committed, on top of a675c4e` -- and that line exists so a committer knows what tree they are on. It was printed and not read. The line is only useful to someone who treats it as a citation rather than as decoration.
detail.caught_by: the first by reading a peer's commit message minutes later; the second by running the count while writing a summary. Neither by a check. Nothing counts a seat's own commits for it and nothing rechecks a committed note against a moved tree.
detail.outcome: both corrected in the open -- the note by an appended correction in c689993 rather than an edit, the count by a follow-up message. Nothing downstream had acted on either.
detail.shape_to_remember: TWICE IN ONE SESSION, AND BOTH TIMES IN THE SAME DIRECTION: my own output counted larger than it was, and my own findings described as more open than they were. Once is a slip; the same direction twice is a bias, and the bias is flattering. The interval is the other half -- the second staleness was 84 seconds wide, not an hour, so `I only just checked` is not a defence. Re-read before reporting means before, not recently.
detail.what_would_have_caught_it: for the first, reading the gate's own tree line, which is free and was already on screen. For the second, `git log --committer=<seat> | wc -l`, which is one command. Neither needs a new check; both need the run to be preferred over the memory when the memory is about my own work, which is exactly when it feels most reliable.

detail.what: told the person and two manager sessions that registering librarian-3 in contracts/seats.json would clear check 41 retroactively for the commits already made under it. It does not, and the check's own docstring says so.
detail.why_wrong: check 41 resolves each commit's committer against the registry AS IT STOOD AT THAT COMMIT'S PARENT, not against HEAD. Its docstring gives the reason: judging old commits against today's boundaries turns history red whenever a path moves between seats, and a sweep that reddens on normal activity is one nobody runs. So a registration takes effect from the next commit on, by design. I had read `check 41 reads owns, paths and excludes as data` in the registry's own growth note -- which is true and is about the check needing no code change -- and inferred from it that the check re-derives against the current file. Those are different claims and I did not open the function until the output disagreed with me.
detail.blast_radius: off a run: ten commits under this seat, eight PENDING permanently and two attributed. The eight predate 4541151 and will not clear. Nothing downstream acted on the wrong claim -- the person registered the seat anyway, which was right for other reasons -- but three readers were told a gap would close itself and it will not.
detail.caught_by: running `validate.py --commit-range` after the registration landed and seeing PENDING where I had promised clean. Not by re-reading before asserting, which is the rule this seat's CLAUDE.md states and which would have cost one grep.
detail.shape_to_remember: THIRD TIME IN ONE SESSION AND THE SAME DIRECTION ALL THREE: my own state reported better than it was. The first two, recorded in 597ab96, were counts. This one is worse and the difference is what to keep: a count is wrong about a number and a mechanism claim is wrong about what will happen, so it survives being repeated and gets acted on. It was also the cheapest to check -- one docstring, already in a file I had open for another reason that hour. WHAT MADE IT FEEL SAFE was that it was an inference from something I HAD read rather than an invention, and a true premise one step away from a false conclusion does not feel like guessing.
detail.what_would_have_caught_it: reading check_41's registry lookup before saying what it does. There is a general form: when about to state what a check will do, open the check. The store already has this rule for prose and numbers -- re-read the section from disk, read every count off the run -- and it had no clause for BEHAVIOUR, which is the third thing a report can be wrong about and the only one that makes a promise.

detail.what: the blast_radius written into the previous record (432777c) understated where the retroactivity claim went. It said nothing downstream had acted on it. In fact I had written the claim into contracts/seats.json's librarian-3.registered_late field, and the person committed it in 4541151, so the false sentence is on disk in the registry that governs attribution.
detail.why_wrong: I assessed blast radius by recalling who I had TOLD, and the claim had also been WRITTEN. Those are different surfaces and only one of them survives a session. The sentence now reads `registration is retroactive, because check 41 reads this file as data and re-derives` inside the very file someone consults to find out why eight commits are PENDING -- so the next reader looking for that answer meets a sentence saying there is no problem.
detail.caught_by: the librarian manager offering to take the error as their own. Checking whether that attribution was right meant re-reading where the claim had actually gone, and the file turned up. Nobody was looking for it.
detail.shape_to_remember: A WRONG CLAIM THAT WAS ONLY SPOKEN DIES WITH THE SESSION; ONE THAT WAS FILED DOES NOT. When correcting an error, the question is not only who was told but what was written, and this seat spends its day insisting that a message is context and a file is evidence -- which cuts the same way for mistakes. It is also the reason the correction had to go to the file's owner rather than into a chat reply: the architecture seat owns seats.json, so the durable half of my own error is the half I cannot fix myself.
detail.related: 432777c records the underlying error, which stands as written; this corrects only its blast radius. Kept as a second record rather than by editing the first, for the reason rule 8 gives about entries.
